Style enforcement runs as one loop. Tier 0 primes the writer, and each later tier passes on only the blocks it could not settle. Reviewer agents then check each change before a rollout writes it.

steps.text: Style Enforcement Tiers
Tier 0 Prime the Writer
Give the writer STE and the house style before it writes
Tier 1 Lint the Draft
Flag findings with deterministic rules and autofix the safe cases for free
Tier 2 Judge Each Block
Ask Jev one cached yes-or-no question per block
Tier 3 Rewrite Failing Blocks
Rewrite only the blocks that still fail with a cheap model
Give the blocks that Tier 3 declines to Opus editor agents
Review and Apply the Changes
Write only the changes that three reviewer agents approve
Audit every written block on disk
Tiers 1 to 3 trust nothing from Tier 0 and check every block the writer produced.

text.insert: The rewrite prompt and the sweep keep each rewrite small and at the sentence level.
Tier 3 never makes bullets, so every rewrite stays one block.
op replaces the text of one block.
Sentence length, semicolons, em dashes, and passive voice can start a rewrite.
finding alone starts no rewrite. It joins a rewrite that another structure finding starts.
Opus editor agents take the other structure findings, such as paragraph length and tense.
The prompt makes the model check each flagged sentence before it edits the block.
The model keeps the author's pronouns and each "this X" phrase.
If the model is unsure, it returns the block unchanged.
The model never splits a sentence that holds a list-introducing colon or ends with a citation.
A sentence that opens with a scope phrase covering several clauses also stays whole.
A short contrast and any sentence under 15 words stay whole too.
To make a split, the model never repeats a subject phrase.
A rewrite keeps every fact, condition, and qualifier from the original block. The checks in Rewrite Guardrails, such as the 20% shrink limit, reject a rewrite that loses content.
Tier 3 accepts a rewrite only when the rewrite passes every guardrail. The twelve cheap guardrails always run, so a report shows every reason for a rejection. The two paid guardrails,
, run last. Each one runs only when every earlier guardrail passed.

props.title: Rewrite guardrails

text.insert: guardrail reads each sentence that a rewrite split into two or more. It rejects the split for any of five defects.
The lead-in clause of a colon goes to a different sentence than the colon.
A trailing citation ends up backing only part of its claim.
Clauses fall outside the scope phrase that covered them.
A piece repeats the subject of the original sentence word for word.
A lowercase identifier, such as a lint rule ID, gains a capital letter.

text.insert: The research pass also listed four quick wins.
Fix the 221 em dashes. This clears 221 of the 225 lint errors.
Rewrite the 28-word boilerplate sentence that repeats on 8 or more block-vocabulary pages.

folder at the docs root. It causes 3 more lint errors.
A lint costs nothing and never guesses. Jev costs little and caches its answers.
A model rewrite costs the most, so it sees only the blocks the cheaper tiers could not settle.
Priming moves the first draft close to the profile at no extra cost.
A primed writer still drifts, so Tiers 1 to 3 check every block.
A rollout writes a change only when three reviewer agents approve it. A bad change that passes review costs a one-block revert, not a broken page.
Rewrites that cut a block into bullets often lost or changed meaning, so Tier 3 and the editor agents change sentences only.
Concise means tighter words, not less content.
A rewrite that loses a fact costs more than a long sentence, so the rewrite guardrails reject that rewrite.
